column1: # Causes found by the LintTwin study, one per disagreeing rule (kind rule) or failing safe fix (kind fix), judged on ruff 0.17.0, flake8 7.4.1, pylint 4.1.3, ESLint 10.12.0, eslint-plugin-unicorn 78.0.0, oxlint 1.88.0, Biome 2.5.15.
# Built from both triage passes (triage/ in the repository); a cause can change with other versions.

column5: reason

Ruff deliberately skips empty `#` lines that belong to a multi-line comment block (45,019 of the 45,113 pylint-only reports are such lines); the single ruff-only report is in pymupdf/src/__init__.py after its block-level `# pylint: disable=all` (line 377), which ruff ignores.

Ruff ignores parameters with immutable type annotations (`name: str = typer.Argument(...)`, `q: int = Query(...)`, `str | None = Header(...)`), which make up the bugbear-only reports (FastAPI, typer, litellm); 14 of the 16 ruff-only are a harness artefact (flake8 output lost).

Ruff treats redundant aliases (`from .m import X as X`, 6,269 flake8-only) as explicit re-exports, as documented; secondary TRACKED: 2,674 unused `import *` that ruff deliberately does not report (#9028); 117 of the 119 ruff-only are a harness artefact (flake8 output lost).

6,978 of the 7,002 pylint-only reports are in `__init__.py` files, which ruff's rule exempts by design; the 26 ruff-only are a pylint false negative: pylint returns at the first non-aliased name of an import (REF).

Ruff's default allow-magic-value-types = ["str", "bytes"] exempts string and bytes literals, which are 156,941 of the 157,523 pylint-only reports; secondary REF: pylint checks only the first pair of a chained comparison and misses negative literals (UnaryOp), the source of most ruff-only reports (246 more are in pymupdf/src/__init__.py, where a block-level `# pylint: disable=all` at line 377 silences pylint for the rest of the file; ruff ignores pylint pragmas).

Ruff's rule is documented to check only explicit `raise StopIteration`; pylint's stop-iteration-return also reports `next(it)` calls without a default inside generators, which are all 59 pylint-only reports.
flake8-simplify reports only when its suggested one-liner fits in 79 characters; ruff uses the configured line length.
Same finding, different anchor: pylint reports useless-return on the function definition, ruff on the trailing `return` statement; about 288 ruff-only/pylint-only pairs sit in the same function.

Ruff's documented exemptions (single-word lines 12,934, trailing pragma comments 7,933, lines ending in a URL 6,639) explain most flake8-only reports, and its documented Unicode-width measure explains 2,295 ruff-only CJK lines; secondary: 2,109 ruff-only are a harness artefact (flake8 output lost, see N806) and pycodestyle misses lines of a multi-line f-string that contains a nested f-string (REF).

flake8-simplify visits each `elif` again as a nested `if` and re-reports the same adjacent pairs, quadratically in long chains (~980 flake8-only on `elif` lines); the rest: ruff deliberately requires both branches to carry identical comments (e.g. a `# pragma: no cover` on one branch); 26 of the 30 ruff-only are a harness artefact (flake8 output lost).
Ruff also reports the implicit-else form (`if c: return True` followed by `return False`, and the negated form), as its docs show; flake8-simplify only reports an `if` with an explicit `else`.

Ruff checks many more file-opening calls than `open()` (io.open, tempfile.*, gzip.open, pathlib), as documented, and deliberately skips `open(...).close()`, opens inside a `with` item, `return open(...)`, ExitStack and enterContext calls, which flake8-simplify reports.
After the re-run: all 130 bugbear-only are bugbear false positives (it recognises infinite iterators only as `itertools.cycle(...)` and reports single-iterable `zip(x)`).

Rule mapping: ruff's PLR1730 covers both min and max, but pylint reports the max case under R1731 (consider-using-max-builtin), which this pairing leaves out; at least 134 ruff-only reports suggest `max(...)`, and the min ones are in pymupdf under its `# pylint: disable=all`.

Ruff deliberately accepts a `...` body on the same line (`class C: ...`, `with x: ...`, `for x in y: ...`) for consistency with Black and ruff format: all 374 flake8-only lines end in `: ...`; 34 of the 42 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts and 8 are same-line `case` bodies, which pycodestyle does not recognise (REF).

Ruff also reports bare names and attribute accesses (1,914 ruff-only), as its docs describe, and skips expressions that contain calls or overloadable operators; secondary LAG: 1,098 bugbear-only Call/BinOp reports come from checks bugbear added in 26.9.9 (side-effect-free builtin calls) and 26.9.30 (arithmetic/unary operations).
After the re-run: bugbear exempts every `raise <lowercase name>` (misses real cases ruff reports) and flags raises in a try body nested inside an outer handler.
ruff checks the syntax tree where pycodestyle matches regular expressions, so they flag different lines.

flake8-simplify suggests `self != other` for `not self == other` inside `__ne__` (114 of the 139 flake8-only), which would recurse forever; ruff deliberately skips negated comparisons inside comparison dunders and in `if ...: raise` guards; 20 of the 24 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts.

Ruff's SIM110 also covers flake8-simplify's SIM111 (`return all(...)`; 85 ruff-only, which flake8-simplify reports as SIM111, outside this pairing), and it deliberately skips loops whose replacement would exceed the line length (77 of the 78 flake8-only suggestions are longer than 88 columns).

7 of the 9 pylint-only carry `# noqa` or `# noqa: PLW1641` (which only ruff honours) and the ruff-only pymupdf class sits below a `# pylint: disable=all` placed in a module-level `if`, which silences pylint for the rest of the module; secondary: ruff ignores an `__eq__` bound by a chained assignment (`__eq__ = __ne__ = op`, dateutil and numpy). (also RF-11, ruff#29422)
Same finding, different anchor: ruff reports on the `else:` line, pylint on the nested `if`, and the matcher assigns these lines to different statements. (also RF-2, ruff#29395)
Verified CONFIRMED (medium): a second loop over the same argument, or the else-copy of a loop, is not reported; ruff gives 3 of the 7 reports pylint's own functional test expects. (not reported yet)

Ruff deliberately reports only `try` bodies that are a single simple statement, while flake8-simplify accepts any single statement; ~800 of the 850 flake8-only `try` bodies start with return (332), if (220), while (104), with (80), for (43).

Ruff only reports `.get(key, None)` when the receiver is a dict literal/comprehension or a name bound to a dict, while flake8-simplify reports every `.get(k, None)` call (sys.modules, self._params, ...); the 4 ruff-only are a harness artefact (flake8 output lost).

Ruff deliberately skips comparisons whose operands may have side effects (calls, subscripts, non-literal arithmetic such as `x == n - 1`) and sys.platform/sys.version_info checks (pylint-only), and it merges runs of equality tests inside a larger `or` (`cp == 0 or cp == 0xFFFD or is_control(c)`, ruff-only), which pylint skips unless every operand is a comparison.
Ruff also fires on iteration (`for k in d.keys()` and comprehensions, 806) and on `not in` (79), while flake8-simplify only checks `key in d.keys()` comparisons; an open issue asks to restrict it.

Ruff only checks `for` loops over names it can infer as dicts from literals or annotations, while pylint uses astroid inference and also checks comprehensions: ruff misses dicts that pylint infers (179) and comprehensions (63), and reports annotated dicts that pylint cannot infer (111); the comprehension gap is undocumented and untracked.

Design differences: ruff reports every updated name of a `global` statement while pylint reports once per statement, and pylint emits W0601 instead of W0603 when the name is undefined at module level; secondary BUG: ruff emits one identical diagnostic per binding of the name (at least 138 duplicates).

Ruff exempts sys.path and os.environ modifications (documented) and pytest.importorskip/matplotlib.use calls (deliberate) placed between imports, which explains the flake8-only reports; secondary REF: pycodestyle takes a string after a `from __future__` import for the docstring (numpy's vendored meson, et_xmlfile) and ignores code after `;` on an import line (dill); 110 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts.

flake8-bugbear only matches calls spelled `warnings.warn(...)`; 257 of the 259 ruff-only reports are bare `warn(...)` calls after `from warnings import warn`, which ruff resolves to warnings.warn (bugbear false negative).

Ruff's B014 only reports exact duplicate exception types, not redundant subclasses or aliases such as `(ModuleNotFoundError, ImportError)`, `(OSError, IOError)`, `(FileNotFoundError, OSError)`, although its own docs describe the hierarchy case.

Ruff only reports a split whose receiver it knows to be a str (literal, or a name bound or annotated as str), while pylint uses astroid inference: ruff misses receivers such as `str(e).split(":")[-1]` or attributes (pylint-only) and reports annotated str names that pylint cannot infer (ruff-only).

Ruff only reports `len(x)` in a boolean test when x is syntactically known to be a sequence (a literal, or a name bound or annotated as list/dict/set/tuple/str/bytes, *args, **kwargs), while pylint reports `len(self)`, `len(obj.columns)` and other unresolved arguments.

After the re-run (lost-chunk artefacts gone): ruff also checks augmented assignments (~700 ruff-only; pep8-naming has no AugAssign visitor) and skips TypeVar/NamedTuple/TypedDict assignments (402, #2085) and comprehension targets.

Ruff deliberately widened the rule: UPPER_CASE names, constant collections and literal expressions count as constants and every comparison operator is checked, while flake8-simplify only checks an ast.Constant left of `==`; the 53 flake8-only compare two constants (`1 == 2`), where flake8-simplify's suggestion is meaningless (REF).

flake8-bugbear 26.9.30 stopped reporting comparisons inside pytest.raises/warns and unittest assertRaises/assertWarns blocks, where an overloaded comparison may be meant to raise; 267 of the 269 ruff-only reports are in such blocks and ruff has not followed.

pycodestyle's token heuristic only checks the name just before `=` or after for/as/global, so it misses ambiguous names inside tuple targets (`p, l, u = lu(a)`, `for s, l, b in ...`; ~400 ruff-only, the other 199 are lost-flake8-output artefacts), and it flags attributes (`self.l = lst`) and names used inside lambda bodies (the 74 flake8-only).

ruff exempts `__getattr__`/`__dir__` only at module scope (PEP 562) while pep8-naming exempts those names anywhere, so ruff flags 12 factory-defined module `__getattr__`/`__dir__` functions (anyio, huggingface-hub, networkx, websockets, matplotlib, attrs, wrapt); the other 5 are in `executing` (no flake8 output).
Verified CONFIRMED: `class Fine_:` is flagged; pep8-naming's tests mark it Okay; ruff#15939 called the deviation a bug but fixed only leading underscores. (RF-14, ruff#29422)

Ruff's rule also covers `with` statement targets (101 ruff-only), as documented, and deliberately skips `x = cast(T, x)` and in-place augmented updates of the loop variable, which pylint reports; 15 pylint-only lines carry `# noqa` and 15 ruff-only are in pymupdf under its `# pylint: disable=all` (CFG).

Documented limitation: ruff only detects built-in exception classes, while pylint also flags user-defined ones (MyExceptionGroup, PydanticKnownError, numpy's AxisError, marshmallow's ValidationError).
All 4 lines carry `# noqa: PLW1510`, which ruff honours and pylint ignores.

Ruff exempts @overload (751) and @override (29) signatures and honours `# noqa: PLR0913` (44); ruff-only: pylint is silenced by `# pylint: disable=too-many-arguments` (grpcio) and by the block-level `# pylint: disable=all` at line 377 of pymupdf/src/__init__.py (109) (CFG).

Ruff exempts @overload (302) and @override (4) signatures; the ruff-only are in pymupdf/src/__init__.py after its block-level `# pylint: disable=all` (89) and in functions under `# pylint: disable` pragmas (CFG).

Ruff's rule only compares a name (or a pure call on a name) with itself, while pylint compares any identical expressions: attribute chains (`transport.operations_client is transport.operations_client`, 208 in generated tests) and literals (which ruff covers under PLR0133).

Ruff deliberately uses a heuristic (a direct base named `Exception` or ending in `Error`) instead of pep8-naming's walk through the module's class chain for `Exception`, so it flags subclasses of ValueError/FileNotFoundError/BotoCoreError (ruff-only) and misses subclasses of module-local exception classes such as werkzeug's HTTPException (flake8-only).

Ruff's if-block check deliberately requires a receiver known to be a dict and a default without calls (`compute(key)`), while flake8-simplify reports any `if k in d: x = d[k] else: x = ...`; ruff-only: ruff also reports if-expressions (`d[k] if k in d else default`), which flake8-simplify never checks; secondary: the docs still call this preview-only although stable 0.17.0 reports it, and that check lacks the dict test (it even suggests `self.get(key, default)` inside a `get` method, pip's vendored distlib compat.py:544). (also RF-10, ruff#29422)

Ruff deliberately does not count the function's own `def` (pylint starts every function at 1) but counts each nested `def` as a statement of the outer function, so counts near the threshold differ by one in either direction (88 pylint-only at 51/50).
Setup artefact: pep8-naming 0.15.1 has no N999 (module-name) check at all, so every ruff report is unmatched by construction; ruff files its own rule under the pep8-naming prefix.

flake8-simplify registers SIM112 on expression statements only, so it never checks `os.environ[...]` or `os.environ.get(...)` inside assignments, conditions or calls (all 55 ruff-only); ruff checks every use.
ruff skips redefinitions inside `if` blocks (tracked: astral-sh/ruff#17555 and related issues).
Ruff only recognises `a < b and b < c` written with the shared operand adjacent, not reversed operands such as `x > 0 and x < y` or `c >= 0xFDD0 and c <= 0xFDEF`, which pylint normalises.

Suppression comments: 445 of the 457 pylint-only lines carry a `# noqa` (honoured by ruff, not by pylint), and the ruff-only lines carry `# pylint: disable=import-outside-toplevel` (22) or are in pymupdf/src/__init__.py after its block-level `# pylint: disable=all` (25).

Ruff only reports counters initialised to a literal 0 (documented) that are not used after the loop and not reassigned inside it (deliberate), while flake8-simplify reports any earlier assignment of the counter; secondary ANCHOR: flake8-simplify anchors on the initialisation and ruff on the `+= 1` (~97 pairs).

bugbear 26.9.9 and 26.9.30 stopped reporting attribute/subscript loop targets (`for self.n in range(self.m)`) and names bound in nested destructuring; ruff still reports these (7); 4 more are in files without flake8 output, and 5 are bugbear's own errors (a set-comprehension-local name reported 4 times, `async for` not checked once).

Ruff reports a chain of nested `with` statements once, at the outermost one (flake8-simplify reports every nested pair), and it also checks nested `async with`, which flake8-simplify ignores (most ruff-only reports).
After the re-run: bugbear does not check `async for` loops (most ruff-only) and flags subscript targets such as `for d[x in y] in target`.

9 of the 16 flake8-only are single-letter aliases (`as C`, `as D`, `as F`), which ruff documents it does not check; 7 are names containing `_` that ruff's `is_camelcase` does not count as CamelCase (`_TypedColumnClauseArgument as _TCCA`, `_Nothing`, `PROTOCOL_SSLv23`); the 1 ruff-only is in sympy's flake8 chunk lost to a crash.

Ruff deliberately exempts `__new__` from N804 (the case is covered by PLW0211); all 31 flake8-only reports are `__new__(mcls, ...)`/`__new__(self, ...)` signatures; 3 of the 7 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts.
ruff only checks sets whose elements are all literals (and skips sets with duplicate values); each of the 16 pylint-only sets has a non-literal element (names, calls, tuples, enum members, `-1`).

Ruff deliberately also checks `os.environ.get(key, default)` (all 49 ruff-only), and it only judges defaults whose type it can resolve syntactically, while pylint infers named constants (`os.getenv("GCS_BATCH_SIZE", GCS_DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE)`, the 13 pylint-only); the rule docs still mention only os.getenv.

Default option: ruff's lint.flake8-import-conventions.aliases contains "xml.etree.ElementTree": "ET" and N817 allows conventional aliases, which covers 50 of the 51 flake8-only reports (`import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET`); the last is `_CustomTextWrap as CTW` (leading underscore, see N813).

Most pylint-only reports are pylint false positives: in implicit namespace packages (directories without __init__.py, e.g. litellm/llms/xai/, litellm/types/, jaraco/) pylint misnames the module and, when it cannot locate the imported submodule, falls back to the package itself, so `from .handler import XAIRealtime`, `from openai import Omit` (in litellm/types/llms/openai.py) or `import functools` (in jaraco/functools/__init__.py) are reported as self-imports (~70); secondary, a possible BUG: ruff misses genuine `from <current module> import name` (13: gunicorn app/wsgiapp.py, psutil tests, rich live.py), including its own docs example. (also RF-13, ruff#29422)

Ruff deliberately exempts TypedDict fields, which are the 886 flake8-only reports (litellm/playwright TypedDicts such as `modelArn: str | None`); all 244 ruff-only are a harness artefact (flake8 output lost, CFG).

Ruff misses a collapsible `elif X:` whose body is a lone `if` whenever the first `if` branch holds more than one statement, because nested_if_body applies the "only child" check to the first branch's body instead of the elif's (91 flake8-only on `elif` lines); the rest is deliberate (TYPE_CHECKING/sys.version blocks, `if True:`, 40) or harness artefacts (29 lost flake8 output, 8 markdown `# flake8: noqa`). (RF-9, ruff#29422)

Suppression comments: all 33 pylint-only lines carry `# noqa` (honoured by ruff), and 79 ruff-only reports are under pylint pragmas (61 in pymupdf/src/__init__.py after its block-level `# pylint: disable=all` at line 377, 18 under `# pylint: disable=too-many-branches`); secondary DOC: ruff counts an `else:` whose only statement is an `if` as an extra branch, as its docs say, while pylint cannot tell it from `elif` (most other ruff-only, typically 13 > 12).

Suppression comments: all 24 pylint-only lines carry `# noqa` (honoured by ruff), and the ruff-only reports are under `# pylint: disable` pragmas (26) or in pymupdf/src/__init__.py after its block-level `# pylint: disable=all` (14); the few others sit in files with file-level pylint pragmas.

After the re-run: 44 flake8-only are methods of classes derived from other metaclasses, which pep8-naming wrongly treats as ordinary classes; 37 ruff-only are functions later wrapped by an old-style `m = staticmethod(m)`.

bugbear's B911 matches any call named `batched`, so 19 of 20 are its false positives on non-itertools functions (anyio.itertools, fontTools.misc.iterTools, more_itertools, a local def in uv); the 1 real `itertools.batched` (tqdm) is skipped by ruff because of our py312 target (secondary CFG).

5 of 6 are `@lru_cache` on `__new__`, an implicit static method that ruff documents it does not check; the other is anyio's own `anyio.functools.lru_cache`, which bugbear matches by name (bugbear false positive).
All 3 bare `raise` lines carry `# noqa: PLE0704` (anyio, pip, pytest), which ruff honours and pylint ignores.

After the re-run: ruff deliberately skips @overload stubs, do_* methods of http.server handlers and visit_* of ast.NodeVisitor subclasses (flake8-only); 55 ruff-only are markdown files with `# flake8: noqa: E501 ...`, which flake8 treats as a whole-file exemption.
ruff checks the syntax tree where pycodestyle matches regular expressions, so they flag different lines.
Same finding, different anchor: pylint reports on the class statement, ruff on the `__slots__ = "..."` assignment, and the matcher assigns these lines to different statements; all 90 pair up.
The difference comes from ruff's dummy-variable pattern (`lint.dummy-variable-rgx`), a documented setting.
After the re-run: the 56 flake8-only are pyflakes false positives (strings inside subscripts read as forward references; names defined through `global` in a function).

pylint skips a `global` name whenever the module binds that name by an import anywhere (meant for `global x; import x`), so it misses 6 useless globals that ruff reports (`import time` + `global time`); the rest are suppression comments (1 `# pylint: disable`, 3 `# noqa`), 1 duplicate name in one statement, and 1 numpy case that local pylint does report.

Same finding at different granularity: ruff emits one diagnostic per `__all__` statement, pylint one per invalid element (all 18 pylint-only); the 5 ruff-only follow ruff's literal-only policy (a starred conditional of strings in frozenlist/propcache, and names/modules in google-cloud-aiplatform that pylint cannot infer).
Ruff deliberately does not report a bare `except:` whose body re-raises with a bare `raise`, while pycodestyle reports every bare except; all 9 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts.

Same finding at different lines: ruff anchors a decorated empty method on the decorator line, bugbear on the `def` line, and our matcher maps decorator lines to the enclosing class; in 4 cases (`@prereleases.setter # noqa: B027`) the noqa on the decorator line silences only ruff.
ruff checks the syntax tree where pycodestyle matches regular expressions, so they flag different lines.

5 of the 7 ruff-only use `typing_extensions.TypeVar`, which pylint cannot infer because typing_extensions is not installed in our pylint environment, and 2 carry `# pylint: disable=typevar-name-incorrect-variance`; the 2 pylint-only carry `# noqa: PLC0105`.

ruff merges only immediately adjacent `isinstance` calls on the same target, so the 7 flake8-only (calls separated by other operands) are deliberate; the litellm ruff-only is one `or` chain with two adjacent runs (2 diagnostics vs 1); 4 ruff-only are in asttokens (no flake8 output).
Verified INTENDED: ruff checks lambda parameters on purpose (dedicated code and test).
Same 3 findings at different lines: ruff reports the `return` statement, pylint the `def __init__` line (alembic 81/72, pyzmq 192/190, scipy 4455/4454).

Ruff also reports static splits with an explicit separator (`"a,b".split(",")`, `.split(" ")`), as its docs example shows, while flake8-simplify only reports argument-less `"...".split()`; 5 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts.
After the re-run: flake8-bugbear 26.9.9 stopped flagging functions that are only called directly inside the loop body; ruff still reports them.

7 of 9 nest a call that takes a generator (`max(4, max(len(i) for i in xs))`), which pylint deliberately skips and ruff reports (its docs discuss the nested-iterable fix); the other 2 (coverage) carry `# pylint: disable=nested-min-max`.
Documented limitation: ruff only analyses classes that inherit from (at most) `object`, so it skips sympy, redis and protobuf classes whose slots come from base classes, which pylint follows.

pylint reports only when astroid infers the receiver is a dict and abandons the whole loop once any subscript (even of another dict) is assigned, so it misses 16 real lookups that ruff reports; the 4 pylint-only come from ruff's narrower matching (only `name.items()` receivers, assignment targets not visited).

All 7 are bugbear false positives: the group name is rebound to `tuple(map(itemgetter(1), group))` before being indexed (fsspec, 6), and an inner `for m, group in groupby(group)` rebinds the name (networkx); ruff tracks the rebinding.

pylint deliberately skips a lambda when a name in the called expression is rebound or deleted later (late binding, e.g. `raises(E, lambda: m.f())` followed by `m = ...` in sympy tests); ruff does not, so it reports lambdas whose inlining could change behaviour; an open issue covers the closely related forward-binding case; the pylint-only lines mostly carry `# noqa` (CFG).

flake8-simplify 0.31.1 (6 Oct 2026) started finding nested returns, and ruff still only looks at the top-level statements of the try body, handlers and finally block; the prompt_toolkit return is nested in `while`/`try`/`except`/`if` inside the `finally`.

ruff deliberately only rewrites lambdas with exactly one parameter that has no default, so the 5 scipy `map(lambda c, x=x, ...: ..., c)` are skipped; the 1 six case maps with `from six.moves import map`, which ruff does not treat as the builtin (flake8-comprehensions matches the name).

Ruff ignores arguments with immutable type annotations, as documented: all 54 bugbear-only defaults are annotated `Mapping[...] = {}` or `Sequence[...] = []` (anthropic, openai, redis); the 9 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts.
ruff checks the syntax tree where pycodestyle matches regular expressions, so they flag different lines.
bugbear 23.1.20 stopped reporting abstract classes that define no methods at all; ruff still reports them, and all 18 are method-less ABCs (docstring, `__slots__` or attributes only).

Mostly a counting difference for the same duplicate key: pyflakes reports every occurrence including the first, ruff only the repeats (11 pyflakes-only); secondary DOC: the 9 ruff-only are repeats with identical values, which pyflakes skips on purpose and ruff reports with a delete fix.

ruff reports a loop variable that shadows an import only when both bindings are in the same branch, so a loop inside an `if` or `try` body that the import is not in is never reported, whereas pyflakes only skips mutually exclusive forks; all 6 flake8-only are such loops (httplib2 x2, more-itertools, mpmath, litellm, numpy); the 1 ruff-only is in asttokens (no flake8 output). (RF-6, ruff#29422)

pep8-naming judges a dotted import by its whole path, so `import IPython.testing.tools as tt` or `import fontTools.feaLib.ast as ast` is reported as camelcase imported as lowercase although the imported module is lowercase (24 flake8-only); ruff checks the last component; secondary, a possible BUG: ruff's camelcase test rejects any underscore, so it misses `_WebSocketConnect as connect` (12); 11 ruff-only are markdown files skipped by flake8 (`# flake8: noqa: E501 ...`, CFG).
ruff is right: it reports `%` formatting with a non-tuple right-hand side, which pyflakes misses.

Ruff deliberately reports only chains whose returned values are free of side effects and that start at the `if` itself; flake8-simplify also suggests a dict lookup when the branch values are computations or calls (`D - C * inv * B`, `"%s" % name`), which would evaluate every branch eagerly (REF for those).

ruff deliberately also matches bytes and f-string literals (aiohttp `assert b"123", data["name"]`, a real always-true assert, and 7 f-string asserts in ruff's formatter fixtures), while pylint only checks `str` constants.
Ruff's rule only checks reassignment of parameters named `self` and `cls`, as documented, while pylint checks the first parameter whatever its name (sympy's `f`, `A`, `K0`, wrapt's `args`).
Ruff deliberately skips tab-indented lines inside multi-line strings (pathspec's tab-indented docstrings, fonttools GLIF test strings), whereas pycodestyle checks string content as indentation.

Ruff's E101 only flags a line whose own indentation mixes tabs and spaces, while pycodestyle flags every line whose indent character differs from the file's first indented line, so a file that indents some blocks with tabs and others with spaces is never reported (5,202 reports in sympy's two ANTLR parsers: two tab-indented lines, then space-indented code); secondary REF: ~4,850 come from pycodestyle taking that character from tab-indented string content (fonttools). (not reported yet)
ruff counts the parts of an implicit string concatenation separately when it looks for f-strings without placeholders.
Verified CONFIRMED (minor): a None (or True, E712) that is the left side of a later comparison in a chain is never checked (`a is None == b`). (not reported yet)

Ruff reports any static value (constant-like and not bound by the comprehension: names, tuples of constants, arithmetic such as `1.0 / 2`), as its docs say, while flake8-comprehensions only reports an ast.Constant value.
After the re-run: ruff checks the last module segment of a dotted import while pep8-naming checks the full dotted name.

flake8 skipped markdown's extensions/smarty.py entirely because of a `# flake8: noqa: E501 ...` comment (19 ruff-only; ruff treats it as an E501-only file exemption, as documented), and 7 ruff-only are lost-flake8-output artefacts; the rest: ruff also checks module-level augmented assignments (`certCnt += 1`), and pep8-naming strips all leading underscores (`__versionTime__`, the 1 flake8-only).

ruff deliberately extended the rule to chained assignments and compares every target/value pair (12 `x = x = value`, 3 genuine `round = round3 = round` / `a4 = () = a4`), while pylint gives up on any assignment with several targets.

The 5 ruff-only are `def __new__(self, ...)`, which ruff documents as an implicit static method; the 1 pylint-only is a function turned into a static method by assignment (`f = staticmethod(f)`), which ruff does not recognise (decorators only).

ruff tracks names across all chained targets, so `x = x = value` (11 statements) is reported as a redeclaration; pylint only looks inside each tuple target and misses it, although its message is 'redeclared in the same assignment'.
ruff checks the syntax tree where pycodestyle matches regular expressions, so they flag different lines.

ruff checks more than pylint: its rule also covers NewType, ParamSpec and TypeVarTuple (5) and TypeVars assigned inside functions (5), while pylint's typevar-name-mismatch checks only module-level TypeVar assignments.

pylint is wrong in 3 of 4: it has no entry for `__next__` in its special-method table, so the jedi `def __next__(self, key)` that ruff reports is missed, and it reports `def __pow__(self, *args, **kwargs)` (sklearn, scipy) as taking 0 parameters although `*args` accepts them; the 4th carries `# noqa: PLE0302`.

All 9 pyflakes-only are pyflakes false positives: metadata strings of an aliased `Annotated` (`ExtensionsAnnotated[..., "one of 'bar', 'baz'"]`, 3), a regex string argument of a call inside an annotation (`constr(pattern=r'^xxx...')`, 2), and triple-quoted multi-line annotations (4) that the typing spec says to parse as parenthesized; the 1 ruff-only is an unimported `Literal[...]` in a formatter fixture (pyflakes matches `Literal` by name).

Ruff deliberately also checks the call form (`self.assertRaises(Exception, f, ...)`, `pytest.raises(Exception, f)`, aliases such as scipy's `assert_raises`), as its docs example shows, while bugbear only checks `with` items.

All 4 are bugbear false positives: it flags any handler that is not a plain name, but a subscript (`except scenario["expected_error"]`, google-cloud-storage) or a tuple concatenation (`except (exc.UnmappedClassError,) + exc.NO_STATE`, sqlalchemy) is a valid handler; ruff only flags expressions that cannot be exception classes.
Verified INTENDED (same root as W293): form-feed lines in black's form_feeds.py fixture.

Both are in markdown's md_in_html.py, which contains `# flake8: noqa: E501 429-433`: flake8 skips the whole file for any `# flake8: noqa` line, while ruff documents that the codes after it limit the file-level exemption (here to E501).
The keyword line carries `# noqa: PLW1509`: ruff reports on that line and honours it, pylint reports the call's first line and ignores noqa.

ruff deliberately compares the alias with the last segment of a dotted import while pep8-naming compares it with the full dotted name, so `import OpenGL.GLUT as glut` is N811 in ruff but N813 in pep8-naming (all 3 in ipython).

4 of the 7 pylint-only need astroid inference of a returned attribute or method result (`return self.zone` with `zone = None`, sympy `self.rep`/`self.alias`, pexpect's Python 2 bytes branch), which ruff does not do; 1 carries `# noqa: PLE0307` and 1 pair is an anchor difference (ruff at the `return`, pylint at the `def`).

All 3 need astroid inference of the argument types (`self.num` with class default None, a sympy Integer for `%i`, attributes in a ruff fixture), which ruff does not do (it checks literal arguments only); the sympy one is a pylint false positive, since `%i` accepts integer-like objects.

After the re-run: 110 flake8-only are uses of names that CPython's datetime.py deletes in a try/else after `from _datetime import *`; pyflakes treats a del in try/else as unconditional (it skips dels under `if`), ruff treats both as conditional. Also 100 numpy reports anchored differently (ANCHOR) and 37 ruff-only `Literal[...]` strings under a star import (with the ruff verifier).

All 5 are `__bool__` methods that always raise (the 'truth value is ambiguous' pattern in langchain, narwhals `-> NoReturn`, pytest); pylint reports them as not returning a bool, while ruff deliberately ignores functions whose every path raises.

Both are huggingface_hub's `line.lstrip("data:")` on a parameter annotated `line: str`: ruff uses the annotation, pylint cannot infer the parameter type and stays silent, and the call is a genuine misuse (it strips any of `d`, `a`, `t`, `:`).
ruff's B002 also covers the prefix decrement `--`, which bugbear never checks; all 16 are `--x` (mpmath, pyparsing, sympy).

ruff's B012 walks only the bodies of `if`/`try`/`with`/loops inside a `finally` block, so a `return` in an `elif`/`else` branch or in an `except` handler is never reported, while bugbear walks every child node; all 9 flake8-only are such returns (multiprocess `elif ...: return`, prompt_toolkit `except Full: ... return`); the 1 ruff-only is in asttokens (no flake8 output). (RF-8, ruff#29422)
A pylint false positive on names used in default arguments.

Ruff reports any truthy literal in an `or` (`1 or g_use_extra`, `7 or ...`), as documented, and replaces the expression with True only in boolean contexts; flake8-simplify suggests `True` for any `... or True`, even in value contexts and when that drops a call (`self.watching and await self.execute_command("UNWATCH") or True`) (REF for the 8 flake8-only).

All 6 use a logger imported from another module (litellm's `verbose_logger`/`verbose_proxy_logger`, lark's `from .utils import logger`), which ruff treats as a Logger only when listed in `lint.logger-objects` (default empty); pylint infers it.
ruff also checks a module's leading f-string, bugbear only function and class bodies; 12 of 13 are f-strings at the top of a module (1 more is in executing, no flake8 output).
ruff reports any falsy literal in an `and` (`0 and x`, `'' and x`), flake8-simplify only the literal `False`; 6 of 8 are such literals and 2 are in executing (no flake8 output).
After the re-run: one flake8-only in an executing fuzz sample (repeated variable key `TargetVersion`); not examined.
Same finding counted differently: ruff reports every constant pair of a chained comparison, pylint once per comparison; all 12 are the extra pairs of two long chains (executing sample, pytest test).
A pylint false positive on subscripted generic base classes.
ruff accepts only the forms of `__all__` that the typing specification allows.

The 2 flake8-only are in parso test data that never imports `re`: bugbear matches `re.sub(...)` by name, ruff requires `re` to resolve to the stdlib module; the 1 ruff-only is in asttokens (no flake8 output).

Ruff only judges `__hash__` return values whose type it can resolve syntactically, while pylint infers that `return NotImplementedError(...)` (1,509 reports in google-cloud-aiplatform's generated transports) returns an exception instance; the single ruff-only is the same sqlalchemy `__hash__`, anchored on `return None` instead of the def line (ANCHOR).
After the re-run: bugbear's identifier test is an ASCII-only regex, and it flags `getattr(t, "__frozen")` inside a class, where `t.__frozen` would be name-mangled.

pylint skips any loop that contains an `if` and bails when a subscript is assigned, so it misses 13 real lookups ruff reports; of the 7 pylint-only, 5 carry `# noqa: PLR1736` (CFG), 1 is a pylint false positive after `term -= ...`, and 1 is a small ruff gap (the comprehension check ignores `if` clauses, which PLR1733 does visit). (also RF-12, ruff#29422)

Suppression placement: pyflakes reports every undefined `__all__` name on the first line of the `__all__` statement, so `# noqa: F822` comments placed on the element lines (transformers' modular_*.py) only silence ruff, which reports each element; ruff-only: ruff checks every `__all__` assignment, pyflakes only the last (black's comments2.py fixture defines `__all__` twice, 15).
The pip case is a zero-width space inside a comment; ruff documents that it checks strings only, while pylint checks every line.

ruff's F823 only looks at the latest binding of each name in a function and the binding that one directly shadows, so a global read before assignment is missed whenever the function assigns the name more than once; both pyflakes-only cases are black's pattern_matching_generic.py fixture (and ruff's copy), where `match match:` runs before `match = a`, `with match() as match:` and `match = f"{match}"`. (RF-7, ruff#29422)
Verified INTENDED: ruff deliberately treats a form feed as whitespace on blank lines (PR #3122), and ruff format drops form feeds too.

All 4 are format strings without placeholders and a tuple on the right (`"... {} ..." % ("a", "b")`); pyflakes labels them F502 'expected mapping but got sequence', while ruff reports the same finding as F507 '0 placeholder(s) but 2 substitution(s)'.
A pylint false positive on async generator expressions.

Suppression comments: the 2 pylint-only are in pyarrow/__init__.py, which has a file-level `# flake8: noqa` that ruff honours and pylint ignores (the harness only drops `# ruff: noqa` files), and the 1 ruff-only line has `pylint:disable=...,consider-using-from-import`.
Verified DEBATABLE: ruff also reports `in`/ordering comparisons with NaN; maintainers may keep it (NaN membership is unreliable anyway).
After the re-run: ruff deliberately skips a name-mangled attribute and a `setattr` used inside a comprehension (it reports expression statements only).
All 4 are in matplotlib's _mathtext.py, where `super` is a local variable (`sub = super = None`, `super = Hlist([])`); pylint flags `super.kern()` by name, ruff checks that `super` is the builtin.
Same finding counted differently: pycodestyle reports E401 once per logical line, ruff once per import statement, so `import a, b; import c, d` gives 1 vs 2.

Same duplicates counted and placed differently: bugbear reports each duplicated name once at the `try` line, ruff once per repeated occurrence at the handler (ruff's try.py fixture: 3 vs 6), and one-line handlers (`except Exception as case: ...`) map to their body statement, so the statement pass cannot pair them.
The one case is a non-ASCII keyword name at a call site (`f(this_is_..._asökdhf...=1)`), which pylint also checks (NonAsciiNameChecker.visit_call), while ruff only checks names it binds.

Both snowflake calls pass a format string containing `%s` but no arguments (`logger.debug("... %s(ms) ...")`); logging only applies %-formatting when arguments are given, so nothing fails at runtime and pylint's report is a false positive, while ruff deliberately requires at least one argument.

All 3 are flake8-comprehensions false positives: numpy's test_nditer does `from numpy import all`, so `all([...])` is not the builtin (ruff resolves it), and the redis comprehension contains `await`, so it cannot become a generator inside a sync `all()`.

numpy's `def __len__(self): obj[0][0] = 2; raise ValueError(...)` always raises, so it never returns a bad value; pylint still reports it (false positive), while ruff deliberately ignores functions whose every path raises.

Both transformers calls pass `max_length=...` together with `**all_kwargs`, where all_kwargs is built as `{"max_length": ..., ...}` but `all_kwargs.pop("max_length", None)` runs before the call; pylint's inference ignores the pop (false positive), ruff only checks duplicates it can see syntactically.

The 7 pylint-only are pylint false positives: it infers that the custom decorator `hides` returns a property and reports the decorated method, which is in fact wrapped by functools.partial rather than used as the getter; the 1 ruff-only is a `@property` function defined inside a plain function, which pylint does not check (methods only).
Misses short identifiers that are destructuring assignment targets (`[ix, s] = ...`, `[q] = [2]`). (OX-8, oxc#27710)
oxlint has no CommonJS scope, so it reports top-level declarations in CommonJS files (oxc#26784, PR #27023).

33 of the 36 ESLint-only reports are .replace(REGEX_CONST, ...) where unicorn resolves a constant /…/g variable statically (it has done so since at least v63) and oxlint checks only inline regex literals and new RegExp(...), a gap known to the porters (unicorn's test is commented out) but with no tracker issue; the rest is LAG: split().join() (unicorn v65 #3048), the RegExp-escape exemption (v68 #3367) and non-static new RegExp(x, 'g') (unicorn >=v74), which give the 6 oxlint-only reports. (OX-27, oxc#27746)

oxlint compares each declarator with the one just before it, while ESLint compares with the last declarator that was in order, so ESLint reports every declarator below the running maximum and oxlint only adjacent inversions (both flag the same declarations). (OX-30, oxc#27746)

oxlint implements an older unicorn rule: unicorn 75 started reporting `if (x) { return a; } return b;` (the 330 ESLint-only), and unicorn 78 no longer reports if/else pairs that assign to a member such as `obj.p = a` / `obj.p = b` (the 50 oxlint-only).

In tslib both tools report the same 31 findings, but oxlint's diagnostics carry two label lines (the use and the declaration), so the greedy matcher pairs one with the wrong ESLint report and leaves 3+3 unmatched; the other 3 oxlint-only reports are a secondary false positive on the declaration itself (a parameter or bare var x) of a name re-declared with var in a nested block. (also OX-15, oxc#27746)

oxlint reports each unsorted object once at its opening brace, ESLint each out-of-order key at that key, so most reports fall outside the 2-line window; per-object comparison on 9 files found identical object sets except one argparse object, which points to a secondary BUG: oxlint skips computed keys with a simple name (`{a: 1, [S]: 3, b: 2}` is ESLint's own documented incorrect example). (also OX-3, oxc#27704; OX-29, oxc#27746)
`// eslint-disable-line no-negated-condition` also silences oxlint's unicorn rule, because directive matching ignores the plugin prefix (oxc#26115).

58 of the 70 ESLint-only are template literals, which unicorn checks since v62 and oxlint does not; secondary BUG: 12 ESLint-only are string values of properties with identifier keys (`{ blank: ' \\t' }`), which oxlint never checks because of an early return; the 9 oxlint-only end in an even number of backslashes, which unicorn skips and oxlint deliberately allows. (also OX-18, oxc#27746)

23 of 26 are the 'fallback expressions' reports (e.g. this.x = y || '') added in unicorn v77 (#3780) and v78 (#3837, on by default); the 3 'reassignment' cases are a secondary deviation: oxlint gives up when a call-free statement such as a = a || 1, this.x = y or x ??= {} comes first, while unicorn only gives up after a preceding call.

All 28 oxlint-only reports are CommonJS bindings named like builtins (escape, Symbol, Promise, a few inside nested functions) that oxlint's builtinGlobals check treats as global redeclarations, while ESLint checks only the global scope; all 19 ESLint-only reports come from /* global X */ comments redeclaring builtins, which oxlint does not read.
All 10 ESLint-only reports are the new 'Combine this initialization with the preceding declaration' check (let x; x = value;) added in unicorn v78.

The 12 ESLint-only reports are //oxlint-disable-next-line and // prettier-ignore comments, which oxlint skips on purpose and ESLint's default ignore pattern does not; the one oxlint-only report is /*jslint ...*/, which ESLint's default pattern skips (jslint\s+) but oxlint's directive list omits (secondary BUG).
Reports a function that refers to itself through the const it is assigned to. (OX-10, oxc#27710)

oxlint skips every + expression that has any + ancestor, even across a conditional, call or function body, whereas ESLint merges only directly chained concatenations, so nested concatenations such as a + (b ? '|' + c : '') are never reported by oxlint. (OX-20, oxc#27746)
oxlint walks only FormalParameter items, so reassigning a rest parameter (...args, ...children, ...plugins) is never reported; all 5 ESLint-only reports are rest parameters. (OX-21, oxc#27746)

13 of the 15 ESLint-only reports have a receiver that is itself a member expression (this.nodes.every(fn), node.elements.forEach(this.visit, this)), which oxlint deliberately skips, and ajv's types.every(...) hits oxlint's 'types' ignore that unicorn applies only to .map; secondary: oxlint reports call-expression callbacks such as arr.forEach(make(x)) (5 oxlint-only), which unicorn has always ignored. (also OX-14, oxc#27746)

oxlint implements unicorn <=v63 (lone throw in a block, in either branch); unicorn v77 also reports brace-less if (...) throw new Error() and ignores else branches (most ESLint-only reports), and v66 skips typeof x === 'undefined' checks (oxlint-only); secondary BUG: oxlint has no ParenthesizedExpression case, so if (!(x instanceof Y)) { throw new Error() } is missed (ajv, esbuild). (also OX-26, oxc#27746)

oxlint treats a class field initializer as code that runs once, so it flags id = ++ID on a module counter (2 oxlint-only, minimatch), and it misses dead stores that ESLint finds (a chained o.p = x = f(x), the last offset++ inside one expression, an initializer overwritten in a short-circuit loop condition). (OX-13, oxc#27746)

oxlint only implements the original `a ? a : b` form, while unicorn 67-78 also reports nullish checks (`x != null ? x : y`), boolean branches (`c ? !!x : true`) and optional-chaining candidates (`v == null ? undefined : v.then`); all 53 are such cases.

40 of 56 are the same findings in long call chains: oxlint anchors every report at the start of the chain, unicorn at the `.concat` property (json-schema-traverse: 19 oxlint reports at line 68 vs ESLint at 71-102); secondary LAG: 16 oxlint-only that unicorn 78 deliberately skips (`x = x.concat(...)` inside a loop over `let x = []`, and concat calls with static-string arguments or string receivers).

Two oxlint defects explain 2 of the 3 reports: x.slice(-1)[0] in an initializer is reported twice (once from the member-expression path and once from the call-expression path, commander), and it is never reported on the right-hand side of an assignment because the skip for assignment targets fires for any AssignmentExpression parent (yargs-parser key = arg.slice(-1)[0]); the third is LAG (unicorn ignores DOM-like .children receivers). (OX-16, oxc#27746)
eslint-plugin-unicorn 78 defaults `checkNaN` to false and no longer flags `parseInt`; oxlint still reports both.
For one five-level ternary chain both tools report once, unicorn at the first ternary that is too deep and oxlint at the deepest one, four lines apart (entities escape.js 10 vs 14).
Misses a named function expression that shadows the variable it initialises through a call. (OX-9, not reported: conflicts with oxc#19461)
Verified DEBATABLE: oxlint also checks named class expressions; unicorn's narrower scope looks accidental.
Treats every unary operator like `-`: `exports.a = void 0` and `exports.b = ~5` go unreported. (OX-7, oxc#27710)
oxlint treats an unscoped rule name with two slashes (eslint-plugin-node's node/prefer-global/process, has-flag) as invalid and reports the directive as naming no rules.

oxlint's boolean-context check has no LogicalExpression case, so a .match()/.exec() that is an operand of && or || in a condition is never reported (all 22 ESLint-only, yargs-parser, brace-expansion, glob); the 4 oxlint-only are LAG: unicorn v66 type inference skips .match(knownString) such as m.match(dir + '/'). (OX-19, oxc#27746)
unicorn skips any pattern that contains a backslash, while oxlint deliberately unescapes simple escaped characters (/\$$/, /^\[/, /^\\\\\?\\/) and reports them.
Same finding on ignore's multi-line arrow function: ESLint reports at the => head and oxlint at the opening parenthesis of the parameters, three lines apart.
Same finding on the same multi-line arrow function as max-statements: ESLint reports at the => head, oxlint at the start of the parameter list, three lines apart.
Both reports are in ignore's setupWindows, which turns the rule off with /* eslint no-control-regex: "off" */; ESLint (inline config on) obeys, oxlint does not read rule-configuration comments.

ESLint's member-expression check reads node.property.name without testing computed, so the variable reference _end in source[_end] is reported as if it were a property name (4 reports); oxlint checks only non-computed members, and the var _end declaration is reported by both.
unicorn v68 added the Error subclasses (TypeError, RangeError, ...) to the builtins that need new; oxlint's list still has only Error, so throw TypeError('...') (json5, uuid) is ESLint-only.

oxlint ignores this used in a parameter default, so ajv's errorsText(errors = this.errors, ...) is reported as a method that does not use this; ESLint counts the default value as part of the method. (OX-12, oxc#27746)

The 56 ESLint-only are `_`-prefixed names (`_i`, `_`, `_default`, `__toESM`), which oxlint ignores by default; 10 of the 11 oxlint-only are in ws, whose files set `/* eslint no-unused-vars: [...] */` inline options that ESLint applies and oxlint ignores (CFG); the last is a secondary BUG: oxlint reports ajv's `mergeNames` as unused although it is called inside a conditional in a comma expression. (also OX-11, oxc#27746)

oxlint returns early when the outer if is itself an else-if, so the final else { if (...) {} } of an if / else if / else chain is never reported (ajv parseJson, ws extension); ESLint reports it. (OX-24, oxc#27746)
Both reports are .some(x => x === value) predicates, which unicorn reports since v66; oxlint's port does not.
Misses a regex whose leading `=` has a quantifier (`/=+$/`); `/=a/` is caught. (OX-5, oxc#27710)
Reports `"Ā" !== "\u0100"` (equal values, different source text), an encoding self-check. (OX-6, not reported: debatable)
unicorn v65 allows a bare export {} as a module marker; oxlint still reports it (isexe, uuid, yargs type stubs).
Misses a setter that returns a value inside an `Object.defineProperty` descriptor. (OX-4, oxc#27710)

In source-map the same forEach/map(function () {...}, this) finding is reported by oxlint at the start of the call and by ESLint at the this argument 11 lines later; the remaining oxlint-only report is minimatch's non-array orig.filter(pattern, options), already tracked.
The ESLint-only reports are in files that turn the rule off for oxlint with `// oxlint-disable-next-line no-console`.
ESLint 10 allows capitalised built-in names only when the callee is the global built-in; oxlint also allows member calls such as `options.globals.Number(value)`.
When the reproducer was re-run before filing, the difference turned out to follow a change in ESLint 10 that oxlint has not adopted yet.
ESLint 10 defaults `blockScopedFunctions` to "allow"; oxlint still reports function declarations in blocks of strict code (oxc#25073, PR #25076).
One promise chain, import(...).then(...).catch(...), is reported once by each tool: oxlint at the start of the chain and ESLint at the final .catch, five lines apart (lru-cache diagnostics-channel).

oxlint skips every function whose parent is an object property, so qs's RFC3986: function (value) { return String(value) } (and shorthand methods) are never reported, while unicorn has reported both forms since at least v60; the oxlint test file keeps these unicorn cases commented out under a TODO, but there is no tracker issue. (OX-28, oxc#27746)
All 40 reports are in qs test files that turn the rule off with /* eslint no-sparse-arrays: 0 */; ESLint (inline config on in our setup) obeys it, oxlint does not read rule-configuration comments.

oxlint collects only the leading run of import declarations and stops at the first other statement, so imports after a statement such as TypeScript's hoisted var _a, _b, _c; are never checked (yargs-parser); ESLint checks every import declaration. (OX-17, oxc#27746)

oxlint reports args.length used as the fallback value in const length = _length || args.length (yargs), which unicorn reported until v63 and stopped flagging in v64 for value-producing || expressions.

oxlint skips any unused catch parameter whose name starts with an underscore, while unicorn (and oxlint's own docs) exempt only an unused _, so catch (_err) {} is reported by ESLint only (yargs). (OX-2, oxc#27700; OX-25, oxc#27746)
oxlint counts only params.items, which excludes the rest parameter, so (str1, str2, count, ...args) => {} has 4 parameters for ESLint and 3 for oxlint (yargs browser shim). (OX-22, oxc#27746)

The file disables eslint-plugin-n's rule with // eslint-disable-next-line n/no-process-exit, and oxlint's directive matching ignores the plugin prefix, so it also silences unicorn/no-process-exit (yargs esm shim).
unicorn v65 also checks directory names, and all 21 reports are resolve test fixtures under snake_case directories (module_dir, node_path, browser_field); oxlint checks only the file name.

For var bindings declared outside the loop oxlint counts only writes inside the loop, while ESLint treats any write after the loop start as unsafe, so a closure created in a loop that reads a var assigned after the loop (tslib __esDecorate's done = true) is missed. (OX-23, oxc#27746)
oxlint ignores `/* global name */` comments.
The 2 oxlint-only reports are the typeof global / typeof self existence checks in tslib's root detection, which unicorn stopped flagging in v66; the guarded uses are reported by both.
`biome migrate eslint` maps `one-var` (default "always": combine declarations) to `useSingleVarDeclarator`, which enforces the opposite. (BI-1, biome#12373)
Biome's rule covers only uses that would throw, as its documentation says; ESLint's no-use-before-define reports more.

biome migrate eslint turns max-params (ESLint default max 3) into "useMaxParams": "error" without a max, and Biome's default is 4, so all 267 four-parameter functions stop being reported; even an explicit ["error", {"max": 3}] loses its max in the migration (same pattern as BI-2's eqeqeq ignoreNull). (not reported yet)
Biome restricts every global name (escape, Symbol, Promise, toString), while ESLint restricts only NaN, Infinity, undefined, eval, arguments and globalThis; both docs show the difference.

Most ESLint-only reports are trailing undefined call arguments (resolve(undefined), getattr(x, y, undefined)), which unicorn reports with its default checkArguments: true and Biome never checks; the rest are arrow bodies () => undefined (unicorn's default checkArrowFunctionBody: true), also unchecked by Biome.
All 4 Biome-only switches end with a // No default comment (supports-color, chalk's vendored copy, color-convert), which ESLint's default-case accepts and Biome deliberately does not support.

89 of the 98 ESLint-only reports are color-convert fractions such as 0.003_130_8: since unicorn v65 the fractional part is not grouped by default (unicorn reports and removes those separators), while Biome still groups fractional digits in threes as unicorn <=v64 did; the other 9 are numeric object keys (10029: ...), which Biome skips (secondary, undocumented).

The 2 Biome-only reports are cases that follow default and share its body (color-convert's default: case 6: case 0:), which Biome documents as useless while unicorn checks only cases before default; the ESLint-only report is in a line that entities suppresses with // biome-ignore lint/complexity/noUselessSwitchCase.

Biome skips an empty block that is followed by a comment on the same line, as in eslint-scope's attach() {} // eslint-disable-line ..., although its doc exempts only blocks that contain a comment; ESLint's no-empty-function reports all 8. (not reported yet)

The 37 ESLint-only reports are loops that also use the index (or declare a cached length like iz = implicit.length), which unicorn converts with .entries() and Biome deliberately allows; the 20 Biome-only reports are loops over member-expression arrays (this.set, codecOptions.encodeSkipVals) or with a brace-less body, which unicorn's implementation skips (secondary, undocumented on both sides).

Most ESLint-only reports are names starting with _ (_i, _, _default) and unused imports, which Biome's noUnusedVariables exempts by design, or unused parameters (pkg, res, name), which Biome checks in its separate noUnusedFunctionParameters rule; the migrator maps no-unused-vars to noUnusedVariables only.
`biome migrate eslint` maps `eqeqeq` to `noDoubleEquals` with `ignoreNull` left on, so `x == null` is no longer reported. (BI-2, biome#12374)

Same regexes: ESLint reports every useless escape in a pattern, Biome only the first one per regex literal, so the extra ESLint reports on the same line are unmatched (iconv-lite's /[^A-Za-z0-9'\(\),-\.\/:\? ]+/ alone gives several).

Most Biome-only reports are parameters or locals that shadow an outer binding declared later (acorn's var code, minimatch's ext, signal-exit's process), which ESLint skips under its default hoist: 'functions' and Biome always reports (it has no hoist option); secondary BUG: Biome also reports a var in a nested block as shadowing the same function's binding (if (n) { var n = 2 } with parameter n; convert-source-map, iconv-lite).

67 of the 78 Biome-only reports are 'The arguments variable is undeclared' for arguments used inside class constructors and methods (argparse, whatwg-url), which is always defined there; plain functions are fine. The rest: SuppressedError and AsyncIterator missing from Biome's globals (ESLint knows them via ecmaVersion latest) and one typeof value check, which ESLint's no-undef ignores by default. (not reported yet)
ESLint 9 and later default `blockScopedFunctions` to "allow"; Biome still reports function declarations in blocks.

Biome reports only the first await inside each loop and repeats it once per enclosing loop, so a second await in the same loop body is missed (postcss 336, readable-stream, find-up) and an await inside nested loops is reported twice (which 59, postcss 316). (not reported yet)

The 110 Biome-only reports are Infinity, NaN and parseInt(x, 10), which unicorn no longer flags by default (checkInfinity off since <=v60, checkNaN off and base-10 parseInt exempt by v70), while Biome keeps the older behaviour; the 39 ESLint-only reports are isNaN/isFinite, which Biome excludes on purpose (DOC).
All 23 ESLint-only reports are concatenations split across lines with +, which Biome deliberately ignores.
Biome declined our report as intended behaviour: the rule flags parenthesized assignments in return statements that ESLint allows by default (except-parens); biome discussion #12377.
All 6 Biome-only reports are typeof window / typeof self / typeof global existence checks, which unicorn stopped flagging in v66; the guarded uses are reported by both.

The 3 Biome-only reports are feature checks through the global object (window.console.firebug, window.console.table in debug): Biome resolves window.console and globalThis.console to the console global on purpose, while ESLint's no-console only tracks references to the console variable.
Same brace-less if statements: ESLint's curly reports at the body statement and Biome at the if keyword, which are more than two lines apart when the condition spans lines (15 vs 15).

Both tools report every nesting level but at different nodes: ESLint at each ternary that contains a ternary, Biome at each nested ternary, so in multi-line chains each pair sits one level (two or more lines) apart and the matcher pairs most but not the ends (20 vs 20).

Biome treats a let declaration as one unit: it reports once per declaration (ESLint once per variable, so let { a, b, c } = x gives 3 vs 1) and stays silent when any variable of the declaration is reassigned (ESLint's default destructuring: 'any' still reports the others, as in argparse's let [prog, ...] = ...); chokidar's case is Biome's documented inner-function caveat.
Biome also checks `forEach` callbacks, as its documentation states; ESLint's `checkForEach` defaults to false.
All 6 ESLint-only arrow bodies contain a comment (// @ts-ignore, explanatory line comments, comments inside the returned object), which Biome deliberately leaves alone.

Biome does not check parameters bound by destructuring, so cwd = toPath(cwd) in function ({ cwd = ... } = {}), v = ... in ([k, v]) => and minimatch's ([$0, ext = '']) are ESLint-only (11 of 12); the last one is the var-in-block scoping issue seen in noShadow (iconv-lite). (not reported yet)

The 33 ESLint-only reports are unicorn/new-for-builtins findings on Error(), TypeError(), Array() and Object(), which Biome reports under useConsistentBuiltinInstantiation rather than under this rule (it covers only builtins that require new, plus BigInt/Symbol); note that biome migrate eslint maps unicorn/new-for-builtins to this rule alone, so a migrated config loses those checks (possible migrator report, like BI-1).
Same three lonely ifs (argparse, yargs-parser, ws): Biome reports at the else keyword and ESLint at the inner if, which is 3 to 6 lines further down because comments sit between them.

The 35 Biome-only reports are Error(), TypeError(), Object(), Array() and RegExp() without new, which Biome's rule enforces in addition to no-new-wrappers; ESLint reports the same calls under unicorn/new-for-builtins, which our pairing (the first rule biome migrate eslint emits) maps to noInvalidBuiltinInstantiation instead.

Biome reports every use of arguments, including the non-computed member access arguments.length (48 of 52), which ESLint's prefer-rest-params deliberately allows, although Biome lists the rule as the same. (not reported yet)
Same regexes: ESLint reports one diagnostic per regex listing all control characters, Biome one per control character, so the extra per-character Biome reports are unmatched (22).

6 of the 10 Biome-only reports rethrow user-defined errors (new ArgumentTypeError(...), new PrettyFormatPluginError(...)), which ESLint checks only if listed in errorClassNames (default []), while Biome checks any thrown new X(); the other 4 are catch clauses without a parameter, which Biome reports with its default requireCatchParameter: true (ESLint default false), and biome migrate eslint drops even an explicit requireCatchParameter: false.

Biome skips async arrow functions with an expression body (p-limit's (async () => function_(...arguments_))()), because the rule returns early when the body has no statement list; ESLint's require-await reports them, and Biome reports the same arrow with a block body. (not reported yet)

737 of the 782 Biome-only reports are TypeScript's parenthesized indirect calls (0, fn)(), which ESLint's default allowInParentheses: true accepts; Biome documents parenthesized sequences as invalid and has no such option (it is still listed as 'Same as no-sequences').

Biome treats exports as a read-only global and reports the common CommonJS idiom module.exports = exports = X (ajv, semver, whatwg-url), even in a .cjs file, where exports is the module wrapper's parameter and assigning it is legal; ESLint (CommonJS scope, exports writable) does not report. (not reported yet)

Biome reports the standard identifier-part class [$_\u200C\u200D\p{ID_Continue}] (js-tokens, path-to-regexp) as a joined character sequence although the ZWJ is followed by a property escape, not a character, so nothing is joined; ESLint reports a ZWJ only between two characters. The single ESLint-only report is an escaped combining mark (ajv), which ESLint checks by default (allowEscape: false). (not reported yet)
`noSetterReturn` misses a returning setter inside an `Object.defineProperty` descriptor (as oxlint, OX-4). (BI-3, biome#12375)
All 3 Biome-only reports are the any-character idiom [^] (js-tokens, postcss), which Biome reports by design and ESLint lists as correct code.

Biome misses a negated test when it is parenthesized, as in json5's (propertyString !== undefined) ? propertyString : 'null'; the same ternary without parentheses is reported by both. (not reported yet)

The one Biome-only report is semver's case '>': that ends in a /* fallthrough */ comment, which ESLint's default commentPattern accepts and Biome deliberately does not support (it relies on biome-ignore suppressions).

The one ESLint-only report is the range check if (0 <= number && number < intToCharMap.length) in source-map, which Biome exempts as a range expression while ESLint's yoda reports it (exceptRange is off by default, and ESLint requires literal bounds for it anyway); note that Biome applies the exemption in if tests but not in const r = 0 <= n && n < m.

ESLint reports 'Unexpected duplicate super()' for a constructor that calls super once in return super(INTERNAL).then(...) (source-map, 2 reports): its ReturnStatement handler marks the path as having called super() before the super(...) call inside the return argument exits, so the real call looks like a second one; Biome is right not to report.

Same sparse arrays in qs tests: ESLint reports each hole (one report per extra comma) and Biome one diagnostic per array, so after pairing one report per array the remaining ESLint per-hole reports are unmatched (ESLint runs with inline config off for Biome, so the /* eslint no-sparse-arrays: 0 */ comment does not apply).
Same literal chains (whatwg-url, minimatch): ESLint reports every + between two literals and Biome one diagnostic per chain, so 'a' + 'b' + 'c' gives 2 ESLint reports and 1 Biome report.

All 7 ESLint-only reports are Error(...) calls outside a throw statement (yargs-parser's error = Error(...)), which unicorn has reported since v53 (all call expressions); Biome's port (added in 1.8) checks only throw Error(...).

All 28 Biome-only reports are !!x used as an operand of && or || inside a condition (lru-cache, yallist), which ESLint reports only with enforceForInnerExpressions: true (default false); Biome always checks inner expressions and has no such option.
